metadata.title: Newton's Third Law: The Horse-Cart Paradox
metadata.register: formal, undergrad/grad audience, no casual narration, no doodle asides
metadata.branding: none — unbranded, book content only, no channel/logo/handle

beats.narration_text: A horse pulls a cart forward, and the cart pulls back on the horse just as hard. So how does anything move at all?
beats.new_visual_element: Short-only question card: the driving question appears centered on screen in ink text with a crimson underline, posed before any explanation begins.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: question card faded out, blank cream background

beats.narration_text: A horse pulls a cart forward with five hundred newtons of force. By Newton's third law, the cart pulls back on the horse with exactly five hundred newtons. Equal in size, opposite in direction. So how does anything move at all?
beats.new_visual_element: A horse and a cart, connected by a rope. A crimson arrow labeled 500 N points from the horse toward the cart. A second crimson arrow, also labeled 500 N, points from the cart back toward the horse. Both appear at once.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: horse and cart connected by rope, two equal opposite crimson force arrows between them

beats.narration_text: If we simply add these two forces together, they cancel out completely. Five hundred newtons forward, five hundred newtons backward, net zero. That is the trap.
beats.new_visual_element: The two crimson arrows slide toward each other and collapse into a crossed-out zero at the midpoint.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: the two force arrows have collapsed into a crossed-out zero between horse and cart

beats.narration_text: Newton's third law pairs act on two different objects, and that changes everything. This five hundred newton pair splits across two separate free-body diagrams: one arrow lives on the horse, the other lives on the cart. They never appear in the same sum.
beats.new_visual_element: The screen splits into two panels with a divider between them. The left panel isolates the horse: a crimson arrow (500 N, the cart's backward pull) and a teal arrow (600 N, the ground's forward push on its hooves). The right panel isolates the cart: a crimson arrow (500 N, the horse's forward pull) and a teal arrow (200 N, rolling resistance, pointing backward). Each panel is labeled.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: two labeled free-body panels, horse on the left with crimson+teal arrows, cart on the right with crimson+teal arrows

beats.narration_text: Only forces acting on the same object add together. On the horse, the ground's push beats the cart's pull, leaving a net forward force. On the cart, the horse's pull beats rolling resistance, also leaving a net forward force. Both point the same way.
beats.new_visual_element: In the left panel, the crimson and teal arrows on the horse combine into a single gold net arrow labeled 100 N forward. In the right panel, the crimson and teal arrows on the cart combine into a single gold net arrow labeled 300 N forward.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: both panels now show a single gold net-force arrow pointing forward

beats.narration_text: The divider dissolves, and the horse and cart move forward together as one connected system. Action-reaction pairs are always equal and opposite, but they never sit inside the same free-body diagram, and that is exactly why the system accelerates.
beats.new_visual_element: The panel divider fades out. Horse and cart, rope taut, move forward together across the frame. A gold-highlighted line of text beneath reads: action-reaction pairs act on different objects, so they never cancel.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: final held frame: horse and cart together, rope taut, gold-highlighted punchline text beneath
